newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysian ringgit slides to 16-month low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysian ringgit slides to 16-month low.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit slid 1.8 percent to a 16-month low against the dollar on Monday as speculators sold the currency on talk that the central bank may not heavily intervene, dealers said.
The ringgit hit a low of 2.5500/10 to a dollar, its weakest level since February 29, 1996. By midday, it was trading around 2.5375/95 after closing on Friday in Kuala Lumpur at 2.5042/52.

Dealers said the Bank Negara Malaysia was believed to have provided token resistance, selling dollars at around 2.5500. Bank Negara officials were not available for comment. The central bank usually does not comment on its open market operations.
"It was a half-hearted intervention. I think Negara was in just to slow down the fall rather than stop the flow," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
"Hong Kong, Sydney and Singapore are heavily selling the ringgit after talk that Bank Negara has lifted orders to sell the dollar," he said.

Dealers said the Philippines Central Bank's move to allow the peso to trade in a wider range against the dollar on Friday, which is seen as a de facto devaluation, has exerted greater pressures on the ringgit as well as the rupiah.
Dealers and analysts said Bank Negara may be allowing market forces to dictate the spot's value rather than defend the ringgit aggressively "for a lost cause".

"Seen as conceding defeat by speculators, Bank Negara may allow them to play among themselves and with Malaysia's good fundamentals, the ringgit will in time be fairly valued," said Sani Hamid, market analyst at research house MMS International.
He said the central bank has realised that it was playing to the speculators' game plan.
"The speculators want Bank Negara to hike interest rates and they make money from it," he said.
Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don last Wednesday warned of tough steps, including increasing interest rates, to curb speculation in the ringgit.
The central bank spent more than $1 billion last week to help the ringgit rise from 2.5250 to 2.4750 to a dollar.
Analysts said there was talk that the ringgit would be allowed to depreciate by 10 percent or to 2.73 to a dollar.
But few in the market would actually feel comfortable to take the ringgit aggressively through 2.5500, they said.

"The underlying macro picture would actually allow the ringgit to bounce stronger once the present feeding frenzy is over, an option seemingly not open to the likes of the Philippine peso and Thai baht," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at research house I.D.E.A.
Analysts have said that speculators would be targetting the ringgit next after forcing two central banks of the region to devalue their currencies.
But a ringgit devaluation was unlikely, they said.
"Although there was talk that the authorities have stopped supporting the ringgit, we doubt its validity," Koh said.

He said with Malaysia's import content ratio of more than 50 percent, compared with 20-30 percent for the Philippines and Thailand, he doubted the authorities will allow the ringgit to slip by as much as the rumoured 10 percent depreciation.
"Our bottomline is that the ringgit is not a candidate for devaluation, but that realistically, in the current climate will clearly come under more pressure," Koh said.

"It may make more sense for the central bank to let the market have its head and actually trust in the fundamental underpinnings of the economy to make sure that this forex selldown is short-lived," he added.
Dealers and analysts said Bank Negara may have something up its sleeves and is waiting to hit speculators at an appropriate time.
They said the central bank still has its second line of defence -- foreign exchange controls -- to fall back on.
